title: Athena and Practical Wisdom
text: Greek myth associates Athena with wisdom, skilled craft, and disciplined warfare. She often helps heroes by offering a plan rather than removing every danger. Myths about gods were told in many versions, so Athena's character changes from story to story. She is a figure of legend, not history.
context: A mythological profile with an explicit distinction from history.
vocabulary: associates: connects in thought
disciplined: controlled and trained
source: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

references.citation: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

title: Theseus and the Thread
text: In one Greek myth, Theseus enters the Labyrinth to face the Minotaur. Ariadne gives him a thread so he can mark the path back. The monster and maze belong to legend, yet the story preserves a practical idea: when entering a confusing problem, plan the return before rushing forward.
context: A non-graphic retelling of a Greek myth with several ancient variants.
vocabulary: labyrinth: a complicated maze
variant: a different form of a story

title: The Gift of Fire
text: The myth of Prometheus tells of a Titan who brings fire to humanity against Zeus's command. Fire stands for warmth and cooking, but also for technology and dangerous power. The story asks whether knowledge can be separated from responsibility. It is a mythic question that remains useful today.
context: An interpretation of a Greek creation myth, not a factual origin of fire.
vocabulary: Titan: an elder divine being in Greek myth
symbolism: using one thing to represent another
source: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

references.citation: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

title: Perseus Uses a Reflection
text: According to myth, Medusa's gaze turned observers to stone. Perseus avoided looking directly at her by using a polished shield as a mirror. The adventure is fantastic rather than historical. Its enduring image celebrates indirect thinking: a problem may become manageable when viewed from a safer angle.
context: A deliberately non-graphic summary of the Perseus legend.
vocabulary: fantastic: belonging to fantasy
indirect: not following the most direct course

title: Daedalus the Inventor
text: Daedalus appears in Greek legend as a master designer. Stories credit him with the Labyrinth and with wings made for escape. His inventions solve one problem but create new dangers when judgment fails. The myths treat technical brilliance as powerful, while warning that skill without wisdom is incomplete.
context: A thematic synthesis of several myths about Daedalus.
vocabulary: technical: relating to practical skill
brilliance: exceptional talent
source: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

references.citation: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

title: The Labors of Heracles
text: Greek storytellers gave Heracles a series of seemingly impossible labors. He sometimes succeeded through strength, but at other times through patience, tools, or help. Details vary among ancient sources. The cycle suggests that endurance means changing one's approach, not merely repeating the same effort harder.
context: A non-graphic overview of a varied mythic tradition.
vocabulary: endurance: the power to continue
cycle: a group of connected stories
source: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

references.citation: Original synthesis of public-domain Greek myths

title: Apollo and the Oracle at Delphi
text: In Greek religion, Apollo was linked with music, healing, archery, and prophecy. At Delphi, a priestess called the Pythia delivered responses believed to come from him. The answers could be difficult to interpret. Leaders who asked for certainty still had to think carefully and accept responsibility for their choices.
context: A concise account of Apollo's roles and the Delphic oracle in Greek tradition.
vocabulary: prophecy: a message about what may happen
interpret: explain the meaning of something
source: Original summary based on Theoi Greek Mythology, Apollo

title: Hermes the Infant Trickster
text: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes tells a playful myth about the god as a remarkable newborn. He invents the lyre from a tortoise shell, steals Apollo's cattle, and hides their trail. When confronted, he argues boldly and finally offers Apollo the lyre. The brothers are reconciled, and Hermes gains new duties as messenger and guide. The tale explains divine symbols while celebrating quick invention, but it does not present stealing as an ordinary rule for human behavior.
context: A clearly labeled myth based on the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
vocabulary: reconciled: restored to friendly relations
symbol: something that represents a larger idea
source: Original summary based on Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes, translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White (public domain), Theoi Texts Library

references.citation: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes, translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White (public domain), Theoi Texts Library

title: Demeter, Persephone, and Return
text: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Hades takes Persephone to the underworld, and her mother Demeter searches in grief. Crops fail while the goddess of grain refuses her gifts. Zeus finally arranges Persephone's return, but because she has eaten in the underworld, she must spend part of each year there. The myth became connected with seasonal change and the mysteries at Eleusis, although it is not a scientific account of seasons. Ancient worshippers could hear in it both the fear of separation and the hope of reunion.
context: A non-graphic summary of a Greek myth, distinguished from scientific explanation.
vocabulary: mysteries: secret religious rites for initiated worshippers
reunion: coming together after separation
source: Original summary based on Homeric Hymn 2 to Demeter, translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White (public domain), Theoi Texts Library

references.citation: Homeric Hymn 2 to Demeter, translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White (public domain), Theoi Texts Library

title: Why Orpheus Looked Back
text: Greek and Roman authors told several versions of Orpheus and Eurydice. In a famous form, Orpheus enters the underworld and moves its rulers with his music. They allow Eurydice to follow him out on one condition: he must not look back before they reach the upper world. Near the end, he turns, and she is lost again. The story never gives one certain reason. Did he doubt, fear for her, forget the rule, or love too anxiously? That uncertainty gives the myth its power, because readers must examine how trust can fail under pressure.
context: A version-aware presentation of the Orpheus myth that invites interpretation.
vocabulary: condition: a requirement that must be met
uncertainty: a state of not knowing for sure
source: Original summary based on Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 10, translated by Brookes More (public domain), Perseus Digital Library

references.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 10, translated by Brookes More (public domain), Perseus Digital Library

title: The Furies Meet a Jury
text: In Aeschylus's Eumenides, Orestes is pursued by the Furies after killing his mother in revenge for his father. The chain of retaliation seems endless: each punishment creates another claim for vengeance. At Athens, Athena establishes a jury to hear arguments from Apollo and the Furies. When the votes are tied, she decides for Orestes. Athena then persuades the angry Furies to accept an honored place in the city. Their anger is not dismissed; the new settlement gives its guardians respect and a continuing purpose. The play is myth, not a record of one historical trial, but it imagines a change from private revenge toward public judgment, negotiation, and rules.
context: A non-graphic interpretation of justice and civic trial in Aeschylus's mythic drama.
vocabulary: retaliation: harm returned for earlier harm
public judgment: a decision made through a community institution
source: Original summary based on Aeschylus, Eumenides, translated by Herbert Weir Smyth (public domain), Perseus Digital Library

references.citation: Aeschylus, Eumenides, translated by Herbert Weir Smyth (public domain), Perseus Digital Library

title: Three Generations of Divine Rule
text: Hesiod's Theogony describes a rough succession of rulers among the gods. Ouranos fears his children; Cronus overthrows him, then swallows his own children to prevent a similar defeat. Rhea saves Zeus, who eventually defeats Cronus and the Titans. After conflict, Zeus distributes honors and responsibilities among divine allies. This is a mythic genealogy, and later Greek authors told some details differently. The poem organizes many local traditions into one family story, but it does not erase every alternative. It can be read as more than a contest of strength: each ruler's attempt to freeze power creates resistance, while Zeus secures a more lasting order partly by sharing roles and recognizing alliances.
context: A version-aware interpretation of divine succession in Hesiod's Theogony.
vocabulary: succession: the order in which one ruler follows another
genealogy: an account of family descent
source: Original summary based on Hesiod, Theogony, translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White (public domain), Theoi Texts Library
